name: French Exchange Variation
summary: The French Exchange, 1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.exd5 exd5, opens a symmetrical centre that frees Black's problem bishop.
intro: The French Exchange Variation arises after 1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.exd5 exd5, where White dissolves the central tension immediately rather than advancing or maintaining the e-pawn. The result is a symmetrical, open pawn structure with the sole difference being who moves first, and it has a longstanding reputation as one of the most drawish tries against the French. Yet the freed light-squared bishop that so often plagues Black is at last a relief, and White retains resources to press for the initiative.
line: e4 e6 d4 d5 exd5 exd5

sections.heading: Strategic ideas
paragraphs: By capturing on d5 White releases the central tension at once, leaving each side with a pawn on d5 and d4 and half-open e-files. The position is essentially symmetrical, so White's small advantage rests almost entirely on the extra tempo of moving first. This is why the Exchange has long been regarded as the drawing weapon of choice against the French, favoured by players content to neutralise a well-prepared opponent rather than to test the whole apparatus of the Advance or Winawer.

For Black the great consolation is that the light-squared bishop, entombed behind ...e6 in most French lines, now has the open diagonal it always craved and can develop freely to f5, g4 or d6-supporting squares. The symmetry cuts both ways, however: whoever breaks it first and generates activity earns the practical chances. White can inject imbalance by castling queenside and pushing on the kingside, by aiming a minority attack with b4-b5 against Black's queenside, or simply by developing more quickly and seizing the open e-file.

sections.heading: Main variations
paragraphs: The main branching point is White's fourth move. The natural developing tries are 4.Nf3 and 4.Bd3, after which both sides usually complete a harmonious setup with bishops on d3/d6, knights to f3/f6 and c3/c6, and short castling on both wings, keeping the tension low and the draw margin high. The more ambitious 4.c4 immediately challenges d5 and can transpose to isolated queen's pawn structures reminiscent of the Panov or the Queen's Gambit, injecting the imbalance that the symmetrical Exchange otherwise lacks.

The sharpest independent idea is the setup with 4.Nf3, 5.Bd3 and rapid queenside castling, when White intends f-pawn and g-pawn expansion against a mirrored black king to create a genuine attacking race. Black meets these plans by mirroring development, contesting the e-file with rooks, and choosing whether to castle short and equalise comfortably or to fight for the initiative with an early ...Bg4 pinning White's knight and ...Nc6 pressuring d4. Precise handling of the minority attack, where White advances b2-b4-b5 to leave Black with a weak pawn, is the main long-term winning try in the quiet lines.

sections.heading: History and background
paragraphs: The Exchange Variation is as old as serious French theory itself, appearing throughout the nineteenth century as the simplest way to answer 1...e6 without conceding space or accepting a cramped centre. Its reputation as a peaceful, even toothless, choice was cemented in the era of master play, where it was often used to steer sharp opponents into dry symmetry. Modern practice has partly rehabilitated it: with an early c4 or opposite-side castling, strong players have shown that the extra tempo and the possibility of a minority attack give White a genuine, if modest, way to keep the position alive and pose practical problems.

keyIdeas: 3.exd5 exd5 releases the tension into a symmetrical open centre.
Black's traditionally bad light-squared bishop is freed to good squares.
White's edge rests mainly on the extra tempo of the first move.
Reputedly drawish, but imbalance can be created with c4 or opposite-side castling.
A minority attack with b4-b5 is the main quiet winning plan.
Whoever breaks the symmetry with activity gets the practical chances.

white: Develop harmoniously with Nf3, Bd3, c3 and pressure the open e-file.
Play c4 to challenge d5 and enter an isolated-queen's-pawn fight.
Castle queenside and launch f- and g-pawns at Black's king.
Prepare a minority attack with b4-b5 to fix a weakness on d5.
Occupy the e5 outpost or contest the e-file with doubled rooks.
black: Develop the freed light bishop actively to f5 or g4.
Mirror White's setup with ...Bd6, ...Nf6, ...Nc6 and short castling.
Contest the open e-file and trade into a comfortable equality.
Pin with ...Bg4 and pressure d4 to seize the initiative.
Guard against the minority attack and keep the d5-pawn healthy.
